title: IRC protocol injection via newline characters in target.name and object.content
description:
The IRC platform's send(), join(), leave(), and update() methods pass user-controlled values (job.target.name, job.object.content, job.actor.name) directly into IRC raw commands using template literals (e.g. `PRIVMSG ${job.target.name} :${job.object.content}`) without sanitizing newline characters (
, 
). While  bypass is already known (#8 via irc-socket-sasl raw()), 
 alone in a template literal raw() call also injects additional IRC commands since IRC uses CRLF line endings and many servers accept bare LF. An attacker can inject a newline into the target name or message content to execute arbitrary IRC commands (PRIVMSG to other channels, JOIN, QUIT, OPER, etc.) in the context of the authenticated session.
impact: An authenticated Sockethub user can send crafted ActivityStreams messages where target.name or object.content contains newline characters, causing the IRC client to execute arbitrary IRC protocol commands. This enables: impersonation (PRIVMSG to any channel/user), channel operations (JOIN/PART/KICK), nick changes, and potentially server operator commands if the bot has elevated privileges.
attack_path:
1. Attacker connects to Sockethub via WebSocket. 2. Sets IRC credentials and connects to an IRC server. 3. Joins a channel. 4. Sends an ActivityStreams 'send' message with object.content set to 'hello
JOIN #secret-channel
PRIVMSG #admin :hacked'. 5. The IRC platform passes this to client.raw(`PRIVMSG #channel :hello
JOIN #secret-channel
PRIVMSG #admin :hacked`). 6. The IRC server processes each line as a separate command.
remediation: Strip or reject \r and \n characters from all user-controlled values before passing them to client.raw(). Add a sanitization function like `function sanitizeIrc(s: string): string { return s.replace(/[\r\n]/g, ''); }` and apply it to job.target.name, job.object.content, and job.actor.name in every method that calls client.raw(). Alternatively, validate that these fields contain no control characters at the schema validation layer.
poc_video_notes: 1. Open Sockethub examples app, go to IRC page. 2. Connect to an IRC server. 3. Join a channel. 4. In browser devtools, craft a WebSocket message with object.content containing '\n' followed by another IRC command. 5. Observe the IRC server processing multiple commands from one message.

title: IRC slash-command injection allows sending arbitrary NOTICE messages to any target
description: The IRC send() method (line 253-265) parses user message content for slash-commands using the regex /(\/(\w+))\s*([\s\S]*)/.exec(job.object.content). When a message starts with '/NOTICE', the method sets job.object.type to 'notice' and then sends `NOTICE ${job.target.name} :${remaining_text}` via client.raw(). However, the regex only checks for /ME and /NOTICE, meaning any user sending a message that starts with '/NOTICE' gets their message type changed to 'notice', which sends a server-level NOTICE instead of a PRIVMSG. Combined with the newline injection above, this could be used to send NOTICEs with injected commands to arbitrary targets. More importantly, the regex /(\/(\w+))\s*([\s\S]*)/ matches any slash-command but only ME and NOTICE are handled; unrecognized commands fall through without the content being modified, so the original '/' prefix remains in the message — a minor information leak showing the command was attempted.
impact: An attacker can send IRC NOTICE messages (which cannot be easily filtered/ignored by clients) to the specified target channel/user. NOTICEs from bots/services are typically trusted by IRC clients and may bypass ignore lists. Combined with newline injection, the target.name can be manipulated to send NOTICEs to arbitrary channels or users.
attack_path: 1. Attacker connects to Sockethub and joins an IRC channel. 2. Sends a 'send' ActivityStreams message with object.content = '/NOTICE someuser This looks like a server notice'. 3. The send() method detects the /NOTICE prefix and sets type to 'notice'. 4. client.raw(`NOTICE ${job.target.name} :someuser This looks like a server notice`) is executed. 5. The target receives an IRC NOTICE that appears to come from a service rather than a user.
remediation: Remove the slash-command parsing from the server-side platform entirely. If slash-commands are needed, handle them on the client side. If they must remain server-side, whitelist only safe commands (e.g. /me) and explicitly reject or ignore others rather than silently falling through. At minimum, the /NOTICE command should be removed as it allows privilege confusion.
poc_video_notes: 1. Connect to IRC via Sockethub examples. 2. Join a channel. 3. Send a message starting with '/NOTICE' and observe that it arrives as a NOTICE rather than a PRIVMSG on the target.

title: Stored XSS via @html rendering of feed entry title with incorrect contentType gating
description: FeedsEntry.svelte line 51 renders `{@html entry.object?.title}` when `entry.object?.contentType === 'html'`. The contentType field is determined by the isHtml() function in the feeds platform based on the feed item's *description* (content field), not the title. This creates a logic flaw: when a feed's description contains HTML (making contentType='html'), the title is rendered as raw HTML via @html even though the title was never checked for HTML safety. A malicious RSS/Atom feed can set a benign HTML description to trigger contentType='html' while placing XSS payload in the title field. NOTE: The known vulnerability #2 identifies this same @html on line 51 but does not mention the contentType/title mismatch that makes the gating ineffective.
impact: An attacker hosting a malicious RSS/Atom feed can inject arbitrary JavaScript into the browser of any Sockethub user who fetches the feed via the examples app. This enables session hijacking, credential theft, and arbitrary actions in the user's Sockethub session.
attack_path: 1. Attacker creates an RSS feed with an item whose contains harmless HTML (triggering contentType='html') and whose contains '<img src=x onerror=alert(document.cookie)>'. 2. A user enters this feed URL in the Sockethub examples feeds page and clicks Fetch. 3. The feed response arrives with contentType='html' (from description check). 4. FeedsEntry.svelte renders the title via @html, executing the XSS payload.
evidence: packages/examples/src/components/logs/platforms/FeedsEntry.svelte:50-51 - @html entry.object?.title rendered when contentType is html
packages/platform-feeds/src/index.ts:297 - contentType: isHtml(item.description || '') ? 'html' : 'text' — contentType based on description, not title
packages/platform-feeds/src/index.ts:293 - title: item.title || '' — title passed through unsanitized
remediation: Never use @html with untrusted data. Replace `{@html entry.object?.title}` with `{entry.object?.title}` (text interpolation). If HTML rendering is truly needed, use a sanitization library like DOMPurify before rendering. Additionally, the contentType check should apply to the specific field being rendered, not a different field.
poc_video_notes: 1. Create a malicious RSS feed with XSS in <title> and HTML in <description>. 2. Enter the feed URL in the examples app. 3. Click Fetch and observe JavaScript execution from the rendered title.

title: Client-side credential replay stores plaintext credentials in memory indefinitely
description: The SockethubClient stores all credentials sent via the 'credentials' event in an in-memory Map (this.events.credentials) at line 533. These credentials are replayed on every Socket.IO reconnection (lines 748-753) and are never cleared unless the application explicitly calls clearCredentials(). While the JSDoc comments acknowledge this is in-memory only, the credentials (including passwords and tokens) persist for the entire lifetime of the browser tab and are replayed automatically on every reconnect, including when the server restarts. A compromised or rogue server receiving replayed credentials could harvest them. Additionally, JavaScript heap memory can be inspected via browser devtools, extensions, or same-origin XSS.
impact: Credentials (passwords, tokens) remain in the browser's JavaScript heap for the entire tab lifetime and are automatically retransmitted on every reconnection event. If combined with any XSS vulnerability (such as the FeedsEntry @html issue), an attacker could access credentials stored in the SockethubClient instance. A malicious or compromised Sockethub server could also collect replayed credentials.
attack_path: 1. User connects to Sockethub and sets IRC/XMPP credentials (including password). 2. Credentials are stored in this.events.credentials Map. 3. If the XSS vulnerability in FeedsEntry is exploited, injected JS can access the SockethubClient instance (exposed as global via line 1012: global.SockethubClient) and read stored credentials. 4. Alternatively, on server restart, credentials are automatically replayed to whatever server answers.
evidence: packages/client/src/sockethub-client.ts:529-534 - eventCredentials() stores full credential objects including passwords
packages/client/src/sockethub-client.ts:748-753 - replay() automatically re-sends stored credentials on reconnect
packages/client/src/sockethub-client.ts:197 - credentials Map persists for tab lifetime
remediation: Consider clearing credentials after a configurable timeout. Add an option to disable automatic credential replay. Avoid exposing the SockethubClient class on globalThis in production builds (line 1011-1017). Consider using one-time tokens instead of replaying raw credentials. At minimum, document the risk and provide a destroy() method that clears all stored state.
poc_video_notes: 1. Open Sockethub examples, set IRC credentials with a password. 2. Open browser devtools console. 3. Access globalThis.SockethubClient or the sc variable from sockethub.ts module. 4. Inspect the events.credentials Map to see stored plaintext password.

title: User-agent spoofing as Discord bot enables social engineering and bypasses site protections
description: The metadata platform's compatUserAgent() (line 48) identifies as 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Discordbot/2.0; +https://discordapp.com)' when scraping Reddit URLs. While this is functional (Reddit only serves OG data to recognized crawlers), it means Sockethub impersonates Discord's crawler to any Reddit URL, including custom subreddit domains and URL shorteners. This user-agent is used for all requests to Reddit-matching hostnames. A malicious actor could use the metadata platform to make requests to any Reddit URL appearing to come from Discord's bot, potentially abusing rate limits, content policies, or access controls that Reddit grants to Discord specifically.
impact: Sockethub users can make server-side requests to Reddit appearing as Discord's official bot. This could be used to: bypass rate limiting targeted at other bots, access content served exclusively to recognized crawlers, or potentially abuse partnerships/trust relationships between Reddit and Discord. The SSRF guard prevents private IP access but not this form of identity spoofing to public services.
attack_path: 1. Attacker sends a metadata fetch request for a Reddit URL via Sockethub. 2. Sockethub's metadata platform sends the request with Discordbot/2.0 user-agent. 3. Reddit serves content that is normally only available to Discord's crawler. 4. Attacker receives scraped data that would not be available with a normal user-agent.
evidence: packages/platform-metadata/src/index.ts:386 - Scrape requests use the compat user-agent for Reddit
remediation: Use a custom user-agent that honestly identifies as Sockethub rather than impersonating a specific service. For example: 'Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; SockethubBot/VERSION; +https://sockethub.org)'. If Reddit-specific scraping is needed, document this as a known limitation and make the compat user-agent configurable per deployment so operators can make informed decisions.
poc_video_notes: 1. Use the metadata examples page to fetch a Reddit URL. 2. Monitor the outbound HTTP request (via proxy or server logs). 3. Observe the Discordbot/2.0 user-agent string.

title: SSRF via metadata platform scrape using open-graph-scraper redirect following
description: The metadata platform fetches arbitrary URLs provided by the user in job.actor.id. While a guarded dispatcher blocks private/loopback IPs, the open-graph-scraper library (ogs) is configured with relaxed URL validation settings (require_tld: false, line 371) that explicitly accept hostnames like 'localhost' and intranet names. The comment at line 369 acknowledges this: 'lets the scraper accept TLD-less hosts such as localhost and intranet names'. While the guarded dispatcher should block connections to private IPs at the connection layer, the relaxed validation widens the attack surface — DNS rebinding attacks could bypass IP checks if the DNS resolution happens before the guard applies, and any misconfiguration of allowPrivateAddresses could expose internal services.
impact: If allowPrivateAddresses is misconfigured (set to true, which is the CI configuration), or if a DNS rebinding attack succeeds, an attacker can use the metadata platform to scan and access internal network services. The relaxed URL validation (require_tld: false) is a defense-in-depth weakness.
attack_path: 1. Attacker sends a metadata fetch for a URL like 'http://internal-service/admin'. 2. The URL validation passes because require_tld is false. 3. If allowPrivateAddresses is true (CI/dev config) or if DNS rebinding is used, the request reaches the internal service. 4. The OG metadata (or error response) leaks information about the internal service.
evidence: packages/platform-metadata/src/index.ts:106-109 - allowPrivateAddresses from config enables private IP access
packages/platform-metadata/src/index.ts:139-156 - fetch() accepts arbitrary URLs from job.actor.id
remediation: Set require_tld to true in production configurations. Add DNS rebinding protection by re-validating the resolved IP address after DNS resolution. Consider adding a URL allowlist/blocklist configuration option. Ensure allowPrivateAddresses defaults to false and is clearly documented as dangerous.
poc_video_notes: 1. Deploy Sockethub with allowPrivateAddresses: true (CI config). 2. Use the metadata page to fetch http://localhost:6379 (Redis). 3. Observe error or response leaking information about the internal Redis service.

title: Client-side JSON.parse of user-edited credential data enables prototype pollution
description: The Credentials.svelte component (line 28) and TextAreaSubmit.svelte (line 37) use JSON.parse() on user-edited JSON text without any prototype pollution protection. A user can enter JSON containing '__proto__' keys (e.g., {"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}) which would be parsed and merged into the credentials object. While this is client-side only and the user is editing their own credentials, the parsed object is sent to the Sockethub server via sc.socket.emit('credentials', creds), and if the server or any intermediate code uses object spread or Object.assign with the parsed data, prototype pollution could affect server-side behavior.
impact: Client-side prototype pollution could modify Object.prototype properties, affecting all objects in the browser tab. If the polluted object is sent to the server and processed unsafely (e.g., via Object.assign or object spread without hasOwnProperty checks), it could affect server-side behavior including bypassing authorization checks or modifying platform behavior.
attack_path: 1. User opens the IRC/XMPP examples page. 2. In the credentials text area, enters JSON with __proto__ pollution: {"type":"credentials","nick":"test","server":"evil","__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}. 3. Clicks 'Set Credentials'. 4. JSON.parse() creates an object with __proto__ key. 5. The object is spread into the credentials message and emitted to the server.
remediation: Add prototype pollution protection after JSON.parse() calls. Either use a safe JSON parse library, or delete dangerous keys from parsed objects: delete parsed.__proto__; delete parsed.constructor; delete parsed.prototype. Alternatively, validate the parsed object against a strict schema before use.
poc_video_notes: 1. Open IRC examples page. 2. Edit the credentials JSON textarea to include __proto__ key. 3. Click Set Credentials. 4. Observe the polluted object in browser devtools.
